1.pericope_label: News reaches Jerusalem, and Peter is called to account
debates: Who those of the circumcision were: Calvin argues they cannot be simply the Jews, since all the disciples at Jerusalem were circumcised, and takes them for men who allowed no place in the kingdom to any who had not professed the law; Robertson reports a scholar who confines the phrase to the six brethren who accompanied Peter, rejects that, and reads it as Luke anticipating the later controversy

What the objection actually was: Robertson holds that they did not object to the preaching but to the entering of the house and the eating, while Ellicott takes the charge as resting on ceremonial uncleanness
outliers: The agreement of Barnes, Clarke, Robertson and Henry that Peter's being called to account is itself decisive against any supremacy claimed for him, since men who thought him infallible head of the church would have submitted at once

Calvin's observation that the thing complained of was not forbidden by the law of God but was a tradition from the fathers, and that Peter does not say so but submits himself to the judgment of the church as one of the flock
Clarke's report of a long addition in one manuscript, which has Peter travelling towards Jerusalem for some time, confirming the brethren and speaking of the grace of God, before the dispute opens

4.pericope_label: Peter rehearses the vision, the messengers, and the household
debates: Why the narrative is repeated almost verbatim: Ellicott grants the difficulty and explains it by supposing Luke had the two accounts from two different sets of informants, whose agreement he took for confirmation, while Robertson treats the repetition as a mark of authenticity preserved deliberately

How to read the phrase rendered nothing doubting: Robertson reports the critical reading, making no distinction, and holds that the change of voice changes the sense, while Ellicott points out that the verb is the same as the one rendered contended two verses earlier
outliers: Ellicott's observation that Peter, guided by the Spirit, raised no debate of the very kind that was now being raised against him, the same Greek verb serving for both
Barnes's rule drawn from Peter's method, that a plain unvarnished statement of facts disarms prejudice better than angry contention, since opposition commonly rests on exaggerated report
Robertson's notice that Peter avoids naming Cornelius or his office, and that in mentioning the angel's order for the third time he seems anxious to show he did not go on his own initiative

16.pericope_label: The word remembered, the question that ends the debate, and the silence
debates: What the saying about the two baptisms proves: Robertson concludes that water baptism is merely the symbol or picture of the spiritual baptism in the heart, while Calvin, though distinguishing the minister from the author, warns expressly against making baptism a cold spectacle void of all grace of the Spirit

What the question who was I is a weapon against: Wesley turns it against church governors who lay down rules of communion excluding those God has admitted, while Calvin turns it against those who oppose the baptizing of infants and against magistrates who silence the martyrs

How willing the acquiescence was: Calvin takes the ceasing to contend as an evident sign of godliness, while Robertson judges it reluctant and Clarke observes that not all were ultimately satisfied, pointing to the later disputes
outliers: Wesley's outburst that laying down rules of Christian communion which exclude any whom God has admitted is a bold usurpation on the authority of the supreme Lord of the Church
Barnes's claim that a powerful revival of religion destroys more erroneous doctrine than all the fierce contentions ever waged for the purity of the church
Robertson's report of a suggestion that this affair, however skilfully defended, decreased Peter's influence at Jerusalem and helped open the way for the leadership of James
Ellicott's inference that the formal approval given here left the later Judaisers opposing the very church from which they pretended to derive their authority
themes: the church opened to the Gentiles

19.pericope_label: Scattered by persecution, and the word spoken at Antioch
debates: Whether the word was spoken to Greeks or to Grecian Jews: Clarke and Robertson hold the reading Greeks to be certain, Ellicott finds the manuscripts nearly balanced and decides for Greeks on internal grounds, Barnes and Calvin keep the other reading but expound it of Gentiles all the same, and Henry alone takes it of Hellenist Jews

What the hand of the Lord with them means: Chrysostom takes it of miracles, Henry expressly prefers the power of grace on the heart because many saw the miracles and were not converted, and Clarke takes it of the energy accompanying the preaching
outliers: Chrysostom's remark that had the persecutors made it their express study how best to establish the church they could have done no other thing than this, since they dispersed the teachers

Robertson's inference from the verse that the hand of the Lord is Jehovah's while the Lord to whom men turned is Jesus, so that the early disciples put Jesus on a par with Jehovah and his deity was no late development read back into the history
Calvin's rule for how far Christians may flee persecution, namely that they may do so in order to spend what is left of life in spreading the glory of God
Ellicott's note that one great codex reads Evangelists in this place, an obviously wrong reading which nevertheless tells for Hellenists as the word the transcriber had before him
themes: the founding of the church at Antioch

22.pericope_label: Barnabas sent to Antioch, and what he found there
debates: Whether grace once given may be lost: Clarke argues from the exhortation that God gave the grace but they must use it or the gift would be resumed, and denies that any word of Scripture promises an unavoidable recovery from a fall, while Barnes takes the same phrase for a settled plan formed at conversion and Ellicott for the co-operation of the will with grace

Why Barnabas was chosen: Barnes and Robertson point to his being a Cypriot with friends among the preachers, Ellicott to his known sympathies as the Son of Consolation, and Calvin to the apostles' duty of setting churches in order before Satan could corrupt them
outliers: Calvin's warning that Satan, as soon as he sees a gate opened for the gospel, endeavours by all means to corrupt what is sincere, so that the greater a church's gifts the more careful it must be, nothing being easier than to corrupt corn in the blade
Barnes's observation that Barnabas is praised for no distinguished talents but for piety, with the remark that there is nothing on this earth so mighty as goodness
Ellicott's suggestion that Luke was the more anxious to record this praise because he had soon to narrate the contention that parted Barnabas from Paul
Robertson's borrowed judgment that a smaller man than Barnabas would have raised difficulties as to circumcision or baptism

25.pericope_label: Saul fetched from Tarsus, and the disciples first called Christians
debates: Who gave the name Christian: Clarke argues from the verb, which in the New Testament means to name by divine direction, that the name is from God and was probably given through Saul and Barnabas, while Barnes grants that sense is the commonest and yet inclines to the Gentiles having given it, and Robertson holds that the Gentiles must have given it since the Jews would not use the word Christ of them
outliers: Ellicott's tracing of the name beyond the verse, to the tradition that the first bishop of Antioch coined it, to his successor forming from it the word Christianity as against Judaism, and to the heathen misspelling that made it come from a word meaning good, which the Christians accepted as an unconscious witness

Barnes's observation that the name soon became a term of reproach and has usually been so since among the wicked and the gay, though it is the most honourable appellation that can be conferred on a mortal
Henry's turning of the name into an examination, that multitudes take it to whom it does not rightly belong, and that the name without the reality will only add to our guilt

27.pericope_label: Prophets come down from Jerusalem, and Agabus foretells the dearth
debates: What prophet means here: Barnes and Clarke both allow that the word often means no more than a teacher, but hold that these men were under divine inspiration and that Agabus at least foretold events

How far the dearth reached: Ellicott, Wesley and Robertson all take the phrase for the Roman empire rather than the globe, Robertson calling it a common hyperbole and noting that Josephus appears to restrict the famine to Palestine
outliers: Henry's remark that Jerusalem, infamous for killing the prophets and abusing them, is now justly deprived of them, and that the best understanding of scripture predictions is got in the way of obedience to scripture instructions
Barnes's list of four famines under Claudius, and Clarke's narrowing of the date by an editor's note that fixes it to the emperor's fourth consulship against an earlier scholar's dating

Calvin's list of reasons why God foretells his judgments, ending with the observation that the profit of this prophecy appears in the text itself, since it pricked the men of Antioch forward to relieve their brethren
Calvin's report from the Roman historians that crusts were thrown at the emperor's head in the market, and that his fear of stoning made him careful ever after to provide victual

29.pericope_label: The relief sent to Judea by the hands of Barnabas and Saul
debates: Who the elders were to whom the money was sent: Barnes doubts that an office is meant at all and inclines to the aged and prudent members of the church, expressly rejecting Calvin's view that the apostles are intended, while Clarke inclines to the deacons and reports a threefold division of the primitive disciples

Why Judea alone was relieved when the famine was general: Calvin gives three reasons from its particular distress, but rests the case on gratitude, that those should reap earthly things who have sown spiritual things
outliers: Ellicott's observation that this was the beginning of the collection for the poor saints at Jerusalem which afterwards filled so much of the apostle's labours and which he regarded as a bond of union between the Jewish and Gentile sections of the church

Calvin's rule that each should consider how much is granted him, so that a poor man may have a liberal mind and a small gift be counted a fat and gorgeous sacrifice, with his inference from the word for ministration that rich men are given abundance on condition of being the ministers of the poor
Clarke's dry historical note that the community of goods had by this time ceased
themes: Jew and Gentile in one church
